questions.stem: The EMT curriculum describes the airway as divided into how many named sections?

options.text: One continuous passage with no divisions
options.rationale: The curriculum does divide it; treating it as one undivided passage is the misconception this question targets.

options.text: Two — an upper section and a lower section
options.rationale: Correct. The airway is described in two halves, upper and lower, separated by a named landmark structure.

options.text: Three — upper, middle and lower
options.rationale: There is no middle section in this scheme; three is a plausible-sounding invention.

options.text: Four, one for each lung lobe group
options.rationale: Lobes describe lung anatomy, not the division of the airway passage itself.

questions.stem: Why is the airway split into an upper and a lower section at all?

options.text: Because each half has its own characteristic set of problems
options.rationale: Correct. The split is worth knowing because it predicts the kind of problem you are dealing with.

options.text: Because only the upper half carries air
options.rationale: Both halves carry air; this option misstates the basic function.

options.text: Because EMTs do not assess the lower half
options.rationale: Scope does not define the anatomical split, and the lower half is very much assessed.

options.text: Because the division matches the two lungs
options.rationale: The split is a single landmark along one passage, not a left-right division.

questions.stem: On an exam, structure names from the two halves of the airway most often appear as:

options.text: Distractors for one another
options.rationale: Correct. Options are built from names in the other half, so knowing which half a structure belongs to is what separates the answers.

options.text: Answers that are never tested
options.rationale: Structure names are tested routinely; this option is simply false.

options.text: Items that only appear in trauma questions
options.rationale: They appear across medical and trauma questions alike.

options.text: Items that only appear in pediatric questions
options.rationale: Pediatrics has its own differences, but structure naming is not limited to it.

questions.stem: Compared with an adult's airway, a child's airway:

options.text: Is identical, only smaller in every dimension
options.rationale: This is the exact misconception the concept exists to correct — a child is not a scaled-down adult.

options.text: Differs in several specific ways that change what you physically do
options.rationale: Correct. Each difference changes positioning, equipment sizing or ventilation.

options.text: Differs only in overall length
options.rationale: Length alone does not account for the changes in approach the concept describes.

options.text: Differs in ways that require no change in approach
options.rationale: If no change followed, the differences would not be testable or clinically relevant.

options.text: The anatomical differences change which action is indicated
options.rationale: Correct. Same scenario, different anatomy, therefore a different right answer.

options.rationale: Pediatric airway management is within EMT scope.

questions.stem: In an unresponsive patient, which structure is most likely to be obstructing the airway?

options.text: The tongue
options.rationale: Correct. In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the structure most likely to be against the back of the throat.

options.text: The teeth
options.rationale: Teeth can be a foreign-body concern but are not the usual cause of obstruction in an unresponsive patient.

options.text: The diaphragm
options.rationale: The diaphragm is a muscle of ventilation, not a structure that obstructs the upper airway.

options.text: The tracheal rings
options.rationale: Tracheal cartilage holds the airway open rather than blocking it.

questions.stem: Head-tilt/chin-lift is the default manual airway maneuver when:

options.text: There is no reason to suspect a spinal injury
options.rationale: Correct. It is the first choice when the mechanism does not raise spinal concern.

options.text: The mechanism strongly suggests a spinal injury
options.rationale: That is the situation the other maneuver exists for.

options.text: The patient is awake and talking
options.rationale: A patient who is talking is maintaining their own airway.

options.text: The patient is already breathing normally
options.rationale: A patient breathing normally on their own does not need the maneuver.

questions.stem: A nasal cannula is intended for a patient who:

options.text: Is breathing adequately and needs modest supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. It is a low-flow device for a patient managing their own breathing.

options.text: Is not moving enough air on their own
options.rationale: A patient moving inadequate air needs assisted ventilation, not a low-flow device.

options.text: Needs the highest concentration of oxygen available
options.rationale: High-flow need points to a different device entirely.

options.text: Has no pulse
options.rationale: A pulseless patient needs resuscitation, not a nasal cannula.

options.text: Causes a specific problem rather than delivering more benefit
options.rationale: Correct. There is an upper limit, and exceeding it creates its own problem.

options.rationale: There is no such blanket requirement.

options.text: Has no effect of any kind
options.rationale: If it had no effect there would be no stated range.

questions.stem: Your patient needs high-flow oxygen. Why is a nasal cannula the wrong choice here?

options.text: It is a low-flow device and cannot meet a high-flow need
options.rationale: Correct. Its comfort makes it tempting, which is exactly why it is the classic wrong answer in this situation.

options.text: It is uncomfortable for most patients
options.rationale: Comfort is one of its advantages, not a reason to reject it.

options.text: It cannot be used on awake patients
options.rationale: It is routinely used on awake patients.

options.text: It requires a physician order in all systems
options.rationale: Order requirements are not what makes it wrong for a high-flow need.

questions.stem: A non-rebreather mask is appropriate for a patient who:

options.text: Is still breathing adequately on their own and needs high-flow oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. It is the high-flow device for a patient managing their own breathing.

options.text: Is not moving enough air on their own
options.rationale: That patient needs assisted ventilation instead — this is the classic error.

options.text: Is apneic
options.rationale: An apneic patient is not breathing and cannot draw from the reservoir.

options.text: Is in cardiac arrest
options.rationale: Cardiac arrest calls for resuscitation, not a mask on a spontaneously breathing patient.

questions.stem: You reach for a non-rebreather on a patient who is not moving enough air. What is wrong with that choice?

options.text: That patient needs assisted ventilation, not a mask they have to draw from
options.rationale: Correct. A non-rebreather relies on the patient's own breath; a patient moving too little air cannot use it.

options.text: Nothing — it is the right device for that patient
options.rationale: This is precisely the error the concept warns about.

options.text: The mask will be the wrong size for an adult
options.rationale: Sizing is not the issue being tested here.

options.text: A nasal cannula would deliver more oxygen
options.rationale: A cannula is a low-flow device and would deliver less, not more.
